passages.happening:
The LORD gives Moses a new instruction, for “one who sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s commandments” (verse 2).

“If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people, he must bring to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a sin offering” (verse 3). He lays his hand on its head and kills it (verse 4).

He carries some of the blood into the tent. He sprinkles it seven times in front of the veil, puts some on the horns of the altar of incense, and pours the rest at the base of the altar outside (verses 5-7). The fat is burned on the altar (verses 8-10).

The rest of the bull is taken “outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place where the ashes are poured out”, and burned there (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The first three offerings were gifts brought freely. Here a new subject begins: what happens when Israel goes wrong.

The chapter starts with the most ordinary kind of failure. ‘Unintentionally’ means a wrong done by mistake, through carelessness or not knowing, and often not noticed at first. The Bible treats such a wrong as real. Harm is done whether or not it was meant, and a person is responsible once he comes to know of it.

The offering is called chatta't. The same Hebrew word means sin, and a related verb means to purify. Many scholars call it the purification offering, because it is also brought where no wrong has been done, as after childbirth. It deals with the effects of both sin and uncleanness.

The chapter is set out by rank, from the top down, and it begins with the ‘anointed priest’, the one later called the high priest. His sin does not stay with him. It brings ‘guilt on the people’. So his offering is the most costly, a bull.

Where the blood goes depends on who has sinned. For the priest it is carried inside the tent, as far as the veil that hides the innermost room. The horns were the raised corners of an altar, its most sacred part.

Why blood inside the tent? Many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom, think that sin was understood to stain God's own dwelling, reaching further in the graver the wrong, and that the blood cleansed it so that God could go on living among his people. Others, such as Roy Gane, think the offering cleansed the person, and that the tent itself was cleansed once a year on the Day of Atonement. Both agree on this much: sin is never only a private matter. It touches the place where God lives.

One thing stands out. The passage for the priest does not end with the words ‘he will be forgiven’, as the others do. Readers have offered reasons and have not agreed on one.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews points to the body burned outside the camp: “the bodies are burned outside the camp. And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:11-12).

Hebrews also notices that Israel's high priest had to offer for himself: “he is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 5:3). It presents Jesus as a priest who “does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 7:27).

That line is drawn by the New Testament itself. It does not slight Aaron's service. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real.
passages.asks: The law began with the failure of the person at the top, and it did not hide it. Ask how you respond when someone who leads you admits a wrong. And if others look to you, at home, at work or in a church, ask whom your own failures touch besides yourself.

passages.happening:
“Now if the whole congregation of Israel strays unintentionally and the matter escapes the notice of the assembly”, they are still guilty (verse 13). Then, “when they become aware of the sin they have committed, then the assembly must bring a young bull as a sin offering” (verse 14).

The elders lay their hands on the bull's head, and it is killed (verse 15). The anointed priest carries the blood into the tent and does as he did for his own sin (verses 16-19).

The promise follows: “in this way the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven” (verse 20). The bull is burned outside the camp (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
A whole people can be wrong together, and not know it. That is the case here. It may be something everyone does and no one questions. The law says the guilt is real, and that when the people come to see it, they must act as a people.

The elders lay their hands on the bull for everyone. The offering is the same costly bull the priest brought, and the blood goes to the same places inside the tent. The priest and the people together carry the standing of the whole community before God.

Then come words that have not appeared in the book until now: ‘they will be forgiven’. The Hebrew verb is salach. In the Hebrew Bible only God is ever the one who does it. The priest carries out the rite. God forgives.

Israel's neighbors feared unknown sins too. In prayers from Mesopotamia a sufferer pleads with any god he may have angered, confessing wrongs he cannot name. This chapter belongs to a different world. There is one God. His commands are known. And when the wrong is seen, a remedy is already waiting, with a promise attached.
passages.later:
Numbers repeats the law for the whole community, and adds a hard line beside it: “the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD” (Numbers 15:30).

On the Day of Atonement the high priest made atonement for all the people at once, “because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:16).

A psalm prays for what this chapter provides: “Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12).
passages.hard:
If this offering covers only wrongs done without meaning to, what about a person who sins on purpose?

Read alone, this chapter and Numbers 15 can sound as though deliberate sin had no remedy. The rest of the law says more. Leviticus 6:1-7 gives a guilt offering for someone who has lied under oath and cheated a neighbor, which is plainly deliberate, once he confesses and repays. The Day of Atonement cleanses Israel from all its sins, its ‘rebellious acts’ included. And David, guilty of adultery and murder, found no offering laid down for what he had done. Yet he prayed, “a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

So many interpreters set the defiant sin of Numbers 15, the act of someone who despises God's word and will not turn back, apart from deliberate sins that are later confessed. A later rabbinic saying holds that repentance turns deliberate sins into errors. Christians read the New Testament's offer in the same way: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: A whole community can be wrong and not know it. Ask what your family, your church or your country may be doing that it does not yet see. And ask how a people, not only a person, says that it was wrong.

passages.happening:
“When a leader sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the commandments of the LORD his God, he incurs guilt” (verse 22). When he becomes aware of it, “he must bring an unblemished male goat as his offering” (verse 23).

He lays his hand on its head and kills it. The priest puts some of the blood on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pours out the rest at its base (verses 24-25). The fat is burned.

And “thus the priest will make atonement for that man’s sin, and he will be forgiven” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The ‘leader’ here is a tribal chief, one of the heads of Israel's tribes. His offering is smaller than the priest's: a male goat, not a bull. And the blood is not carried into the tent. It is put on the altar in the courtyard.

Leaders are named apart from ordinary people, and their offering costs more. In this chapter, rank raises the stakes. The more people depend on someone, the more his wrongs matter.

The law also takes for granted that a leader will sometimes be wrong, and it gives him a way to say so. An old rabbinic comment noticed that this case alone begins with the Hebrew word asher, ‘when’, and heard in it an echo of ashrei, ‘happy’: happy the people whose leader admits his failures.
passages.later:
The prophet Ezekiel uses the same word for the ruler of a restored Israel, who provides “a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people of the land” (Ezekiel 45:22).

Jesus stated the principle behind the higher cost: “From everyone who has been given much, much will be required” (Luke 12:48). James applied it to teachers in the church: “we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1).
passages.asks: The law expected leaders to fail, and made a public way for them to own it. Ask whether the people you lead have ever heard you admit that you were wrong. And ask whether you make it easy or hard for those over you to admit a fault.

passages.happening:
“And if one of the common people sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the LORD’s commandments, he incurs guilt” (verse 27). When he becomes aware of it, “he must bring an unblemished female goat as his offering for that sin” (verse 28). He may bring a female lamb instead (verse 32).

He lays his hand on the animal's head and kills it. The priest puts the blood on the horns of the altar and pours the rest at its base, and burns the fat (verses 29-31, 33-35).

“In this way the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Last come the ‘common people’. The Hebrew says, word for word, the people of the land: ordinary members of the community.

The offering is smaller again, a female goat or lamb. The cost comes down with each step of the chapter. The result does not. The words spoken over the tribal chief are spoken over the farmer: ‘he will be forgiven’. They come twice in this passage, once for the goat and once for the lamb.

Notice the wording in each case: ‘When he becomes aware of the sin he has committed’. The law does not ask people to live in dread of wrongs they cannot know. It asks them to act when they come to see. Becoming aware is treated as the beginning of the way back.

And one phrase in verse 31 is new for this offering: it is burned ‘as a pleasing aroma to the LORD’. That was said of the freely given offerings in chapters 1 to 3. Here it is said of the offering of a person who did wrong and came back.
passages.later:
David knew this forgiveness: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity”, and “You forgave the guilt of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

Another psalm says, “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:3-4).

Paul writes that God sent his own Son ‘as an offering for sin’ (Romans 8:3). The Greek phrase is the one the old Greek translation of Leviticus uses for this offering.
passages.asks: The same promise is made to the priest's people, the chief and the farmer: forgiven. Ask what you have recently come to see about yourself that you did not see before. And ask what it would mean to bring it to God today and not carry it further.
